summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 11.2 percent of transportation and warehousing firms reported using AI in the latest period surveyed, up from 10.7 percent in the prior period. That figure covers the full range of the sector, from small carriers to large logistics operators, and likely understates deployment intensity at the largest platforms, where AI is embedded across core operations rather than treated as a discrete tool.

The most visible application is autonomous freight on highway corridors. Aurora describes its Aurora Driver as integrating autonomy into commercial trucking fleets, with partners citing pilot results on routes between Fort Worth and El Paso and projections that freight volumes will grow fivefold between 2010 and 2050, framing autonomous transport as a necessity rather than an option. Waymo, which traces its origins to the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and served its first fully autonomous ride in 2015, publishes a safety program and crash-rate methodology it describes as the most rigorous public evidence base from an autonomous vehicle operator, positioning the technology as a response to what it calls an unacceptable status quo in road safety. Fleet telematics represent a less dramatic but already-deployed form of AI at scale: Samsara reports that its AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, and automated coaching have contributed to more than 380,000 accidents prevented across the more than 20,000 operations it serves, with capabilities spanning drowsiness detection, driver coaching, and predictive analytics.

In freight brokerage and logistics, C.H. Robinson describes its Managed Solutions offering as moving customers toward what it calls autonomous logistics orchestration, where supply chains analyze, decide, execute, and improve continuously across every shipment, applying AI to load matching, dynamic pricing, and multi-modal route optimization at a network it characterizes as one of the largest in global logistics. Maritime AI is advancing through equipment makers rather than pure-play software firms: Wärtsilä describes AI-driven predictive analytics as part of the toolkit it uses to help marine customers pursue decarbonization, combining flexible engines with data intelligence. The International Maritime Organization adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, with the code entering into effect on 1 July 2026, though the IMO notes that at present there are no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships that operate autonomously or under remote control, and that the code begins as voluntary guidance designed to facilitate a future transition into a mandatory instrument.

Regulatory posture differs sharply by mode. In aviation, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency has published its AI Roadmap 2.0, describing it as a living document outlining safety and ethical considerations, providing a comprehensive action plan for its AI programme, and setting out anticipated rulemaking activities, with nothing flying commercially without clearing these gatekeepers. Airbus frames its innovation work around a vision of a decarbonized, connected, and autonomous future for aerospace, working with an external innovation ecosystem to translate ideas into breakthroughs. The American Trucking Associations, representing more than 37,000 members, functions as the principal industry body tracking autonomous trucking policy and works to educate policymakers on the role trucking plays in the economy, a function that matters as federal and state rules for driverless commercial vehicles remain unsettled.

For an operator considering deployment, the evidence suggests the clearest near-term return lies in fleet telematics and logistics optimization, where tools from providers like Samsara and platforms like C.H. Robinson's are commercially available and carry documented safety and efficiency claims. Autonomous vehicle deployment at Level 4 on defined corridors is real but still concentrated among well-capitalized specialists, and the regulatory timelines for broader commercial operation remain uncertain across all modes. Maritime autonomy has its first international framework but no commercial SOLAS-class autonomous fleet yet. Aviation AI faces the most structured certification process of any mode. A buyer entering this sector should expect meaningful variation in readiness by application, with telematics and prediction offering the shortest path to measurable benefit and full autonomy requiring patience with both technology maturation and regulatory process.
